newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian shares soften on Western sales, seen down.
newsitem.headline: Russian shares soften on Western sales, seen down.

text.p: Western selling nudged leading Russian shares down in morning trade on Tuesday but dealers, who disagreed on the reasons for the sales, saw support at lower levels and said the market would not slip far.
The Russian Trading System 21-share index opened a half percent down on Monday's close, at 541.64 after 544.69.
ING Barings trader Oleg Galkin said foreign investors were selling on worries about the U.S. market, despite the Dow Jones Monday recovery from Friday's near-record point loss.
"It is more about nerves," Galkin said, adding he thought the sales would be short-lived. "Westerners want to get rid of their riskier securities."
But another trader at a Western brokerage said the morning dip in share prices was unrelated to events in the U.S.

"People are just taking profits," the trader said. "The market has grown well and the correction which began with Dow Jones fall is just continuing -- maybe it's something to do with people going off on holiday."
National power company UES dipped to $0.4360 at 0845 GMT from $0.4391 on Monday, while oil company LUKoil slipped to $26.700 from $27.100. Local utility Mosenergo eased to $1.660 from $1.675.
Galkin said the market was already calmer after a steeper opening slide.
"Russians want to buy lower and Westerners want to sell higher, so you've got a situation where there is no one selling and no one buying."
And traders said Russian and even some Western demand for stock would prop market up at lower levels.
"I think that if the market falls a few more percent there will be buyers," said the trader at the Western brokerage. "There are people with money on hold who will buy -- both Russian and Western.

But Galkin, who said he did not expect any significant policy change on U.S. interest rates from today's Federal Reserve meeting, said the market would remain sensitive to any further out-of-the-ordinary Dow movements.
"As long as there is no news in Russia there is nothing else that can really affect the market," he said.
